content: Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that works by irreversibly binding to the (H+, K+)-ATPase enzyme system located on the secretory surface of gastric parietal cells. This action inhibits the final step in gastric acid production, effectively suppressing both basal and stimulated gastric acid secretion, regardless of the stimulus. Pantoprazole is indicated for the short-term treatment (up to 8 weeks) of erosive esophagitis associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in adults and pediatric patients aged 5 years and older. For adult patients who do not achieve healing after 8 weeks, an additional 8-week course may be considered. However, the safety of treatment beyond 8 weeks in pediatric patients has not been established. The recommended adult dose for short-term treatment of erosive esophagitis associated with GERD is 40 mg once daily, either orally or by intravenous infusion, for 7 to 10 days. For maintenance of healing and reduction of relapse rates of daytime and nighttime heartburn symptoms in GERD, the recommended dose is 40 mg orally once daily. Controlled studies for maintenance therapy have evaluated durations of up to 12 months. Pantoprazole is also indicated for the long-term treatment of pathological hypersecretory conditions, including Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. The recommended adult dose for this condition is 80 mg by intravenous infusion every 12 hours, with dosage adjustments based on acid output measurements. Doses may be increased to 80 mg every 8 hours if needed, but doses exceeding 240 mg per day or therapy durations longer than 6 days have not been studied. Common adverse reactions to pantoprazole include headache, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, flatulence, dizziness, arthralgia, upper respiratory infections, fever, and rash. Rare but serious adverse events include hypomagnesemia, Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea, bone fractures, and vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use. Atrophic gastritis has been observed in patients treated long-term, particularly those who are H. pylori positive. Pantoprazole is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to any component of the formulation or substituted benzimidazoles. It should be used with caution in patients with concurrent gastric malignancy, as symptomatic response to therapy does not rule out the presence of malignancy. In pediatric patients aged 5 years and older, the recommended dose for GERD-associated erosive esophagitis is 20 mg once daily for those weighing 15 to less than 40 kg, and 40 mg once daily for those weighing 40 kg or more, for up to 8 weeks. The safety and effectiveness of pantoprazole in patients younger than 1 year of age or for uses other than GERD-associated erosive esophagitis have not been established. Pantoprazole is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA, indicating that animal studies have not demonstrated harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. It should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Pantoprazole is excreted in human milk, and a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the potential for tumorigenicity observed in animal studies. Pantoprazole may interact with other drugs. Concomitant use with atazanavir or nelfinavir is not recommended due to reduced plasma concentrations of these antiretroviral drugs. Caution is advised when co-administering with warfarin, as increased INR and prothrombin time have been reported, potentially leading to abnormal bleeding. Pantoprazole may also interfere with the absorption of drugs where gastric pH is an important determinant of bioavailability, such as ketoconazole and iron salts. In cases of overdose, pantoprazole is not removed by hemodialysis, and treatment should be symptomatic and supportive. Symptoms of acute toxicity in animal studies included hypoactivity, ataxia, and tremor. Pantoprazole is available as delayed-release tablets in 20 mg and 40 mg strengths. Tablets should be swallowed whole, with or without food. If patients are unable to swallow a 40 mg tablet, two 20 mg tablets may be taken. Concomitant administration of antacids does not affect the absorption of pantoprazole. The safety and efficacy of pantoprazole in elderly patients are similar to those in younger patients. No specific dosage adjustments are required based on age, gender, or renal impairment. However, doses higher than 40 mg per day have not been studied in patients with hepatic impairment.
